text: Design a microservices architecture in Rust.
expected_response: Decompose the application into independently deployable services, each owning its data store and communicating through async message passing. Use an API Gateway (Proxy pattern) as the single entry point for external clients, routing requests to the appropriate service. Apply Event Sourcing so each service publishes domain events to a message broker, enabling loose coupling without direct service-to-service calls. Structure each service internally with a hexagonal architecture: domain logic at the center, adapter layers for HTTP, gRPC, and database access on the boundary.

text: Design a microservices architecture in Python.
expected_response: Structure the system as a collection of small, focused services communicating via REST or message queues. Use a Proxy Gateway to handle authentication, rate limiting, and routing. Each service follows the Repository pattern internally, separating domain logic from data access. Apply the Observer pattern for cross-service event notification through a message broker like RabbitMQ or Redis Streams, so services react to events they care about without direct coupling.

text: How do Observer and Event-Driven Architecture work together?
expected_response: Observer defines a local one-to-many notification mechanism within a single process. Event-Driven Architecture scales this concept across service boundaries: instead of direct method calls, services publish events to a message broker and other services subscribe to events they care about. Together they create a system where local state changes propagate globally without tight coupling. Observer handles in-process notification; the event bus handles cross-process distribution.

text: Combine Proxy and Circuit Breaker for resilient service communication.
expected_response: Wrap each remote service call in a Proxy that delegates to the real client. The Proxy integrates a Circuit Breaker that tracks failure rates: when failures exceed a threshold, the circuit opens and the Proxy returns a cached or default response instead of attempting the call. After a cooldown period, the circuit transitions to half-open, allowing a trial request. This combination isolates failures, prevents cascade effects, and provides graceful degradation without changing the client interface.

text: Use Strategy pattern with Factory for configurable algorithms at runtime.
expected_response: Define each algorithm variant as a Strategy implementation behind a common interface. Use a Factory to instantiate the correct strategy based on runtime configuration, user preference, or environment variables. The client receives the strategy through dependency injection and calls it without knowing which variant was selected. This separates algorithm selection (Factory) from algorithm execution (Strategy), making both independently extensible.

text: Design a plugin system using Component, Flyweight, and Factory patterns.
expected_response: Define a Plugin trait (Component pattern) that all extensions implement, exposing lifecycle hooks like init, execute, and shutdown. Use a Factory to instantiate plugins from configuration or discovery, isolating the host from concrete plugin types. Apply Flyweight for shared immutable state across plugin instances, such as compiled regex patterns, lookup tables, or parsed schemas, reducing memory when many plugins share common resources. The host iterates over registered components, invoking each through the uniform interface.

text: Apply CQRS with Event Sourcing for an audit-compliant system.
expected_response: Separate the write model (Command side) from the read model (Query side). Commands mutate state by appending events to an immutable event store rather than updating records in place. The read side subscribes to the event stream and projects events into optimized query views. This provides a complete audit trail (every state change is an event), enables temporal queries (replay events to reconstruct past state), and allows independent scaling of reads and writes.

text: How do Decorator and Chain of Responsibility compose for middleware pipelines?
expected_response: Each middleware layer is a Decorator that wraps the next handler, adding behavior before and after delegation. The Chain of Responsibility links these decorators in sequence: authentication checks first, then rate limiting, then logging, then the actual handler. Each layer can short-circuit the chain by returning early or pass the request down. This composes cross-cutting concerns cleanly, with each middleware independently testable and reorderable.

text: Design a notification system combining Observer, Template Method, and Adapter.
expected_response: The core uses Observer to track subscribers and notify them when events occur. Each notification channel (email, SMS, push, webhook) implements a Template Method that defines the send workflow: validate recipient, format message, dispatch, log result. Channels that wrap third-party APIs use Adapter to translate the internal notification interface into the provider-specific API. Adding a new channel means implementing one Adapter and one Template Method subclass, with zero changes to the Observer core.

text: Combine Hexagonal Architecture with Repository and Dependency Injection.
expected_response: Place domain logic at the center with no external dependencies. Define ports as trait interfaces for inbound use cases and outbound data access. The Repository pattern implements the outbound port, abstracting database operations behind a domain-friendly interface. Dependency Injection wires concrete adapters (Postgres repository, HTTP client, message publisher) into the ports at application startup. The domain remains testable in isolation by injecting mock adapters, while production code swaps in real implementations.

text: Design a real-time dashboard using MVC and Observer.
expected_response: The Model holds application state and metrics data. Views subscribe to the Model as Observers, automatically re-rendering when state changes. The Controller handles user interactions (filter changes, time range selection) and updates the Model accordingly. When new data arrives via WebSocket, the Model updates its state and notifies all subscribed Views, which re-render their charts and tables without the Controller needing to orchestrate each view update.

text: Build a component library using Compound Components and Render Props.
expected_response: Compound Components share implicit state through context, allowing flexible composition. A parent component manages state while child components render specific parts: Menu manages open/close state, Menu.Trigger renders the button, Menu.Items renders the dropdown. Render Props expose internal state via a function prop, letting consumers control rendering without modifying the component. Together they create a library where components are both opinionated by default and fully customizable when needed.

text: Implement a form system using State Machine and Validation Chain patterns.
expected_response: Model the form lifecycle as a state machine with states: idle, editing, validating, submitting, success, error. Each transition triggers specific behavior. Validation uses a Chain of Responsibility where each validator checks one rule (required, format, length, custom) and either passes to the next or short-circuits with an error. The state machine ensures validation runs before submission, prevents double-submits, and handles async validation states cleanly.

text: Design a theming system using Strategy and Context patterns.
expected_response: Each theme is a Strategy that provides color tokens, typography scales, spacing values, and component variant styles. A Theme Context holds the active strategy and propagates it to all components in the tree. Components read tokens from context rather than hardcoding values. Switching themes means swapping the strategy in context, which triggers re-renders with the new token set. Nested contexts allow theme overrides for specific subtrees, like a dark sidebar within a light page.
